title: Looking back: year five
hook: the sources, the perfections, the householder, death, the life of practice
tomorrow: what's the second arrow, and who shoots it?

segments.voice: Yesterday, year four: many doors, the arahant and the bodhisattva, each in its own words. Today, this year, the year of the sources, and how they reached you.

A grandparent's voice memo can land harder than any photo: the pauses, the accent, the laugh in the middle of a sentence. This year you read the sources: the perfections, the householder, death, a life of practice. Open almost any of those discourses and the first words aren't the Buddha's. They're a listener's. Thus have I heard. In Pali, evam me sutam. Why would the core texts of a tradition open by admitting they're secondhand? The answer is a sound, not a page.
screen: `A VOICE MEMO HITS DIFFERENT.` → `"THUS HAVE I HEARD."` → `WHY OPEN SECONDHAND?`

segments.voice: Tradition says that after the Buddha died, the monks gathered to agree on what he had taught, and Ananda, the Buddha's attendant, who had walked beside him and heard so much, recited the discourses. Each one he began the same way: thus have I heard, at one time the Blessed One was staying at such a place. Not I say. I heard. The words passed from voice to ear, monks chanting them together so nothing slipped, long before they were written down. Chanting has a feel: a low hum in the chest, many voices on one note, and a slip is easy to hear, because the room stops matching. So the sources you read this year were sound before they were ink. That's why Buddhists chant. At a temple, at a funeral, at a house blessing, monks and lay people still chant suttas aloud, often in Pali, the way the words first traveled. The opening is also a small lesson in humility. Even Ananda didn't claim the teaching as his. He only promised to pass it on as he heard it. And that's what you did all year. The sources came to you secondhand, through many voices, and you heard them.
screen: `ANANDA RECITES WHAT HE HEARD.` · `NOT "I SAY." "I HEARD."` · `SOUND BEFORE INK.` · `WHY BUDDHISTS STILL CHANT.` · then, large: `THE SOURCES.`

segments.voice: Find the quietest steady sound around you: a fan, a fridge, rain, your own breath. Listen to it the whole way through the sit, the way Ananda's listeners listened, with nothing to add. At the end, if you like, say softly the words every sutta hands down: evam me sutam, thus have I heard.
Looking back, at year five: the sources, which reached you the way they reached everyone, as something heard.
Your line: the sources, heard before they were read. Five years looked back on, one day at a time.

fork.setup: your friend says a teaching that was passed on by memory for generations can't be trusted. what does the opening line of a sutta say back?

notes: Rhys Davids' DN 1 opens 'Thus have I heard.' Confirm exact wording and punctuation; otherwise switch to a paraphrase.

Cullavagga 11 paraphrased: the first council after the Buddha's passing; Ananda questioned on the discourses. 'Heard more than anyone' follows the tradition that Ananda was foremost among the learned (AN 1, etadagga); confirm or soften. No dates or counts given for the oral period or the writing down.
'Open almost any of those discourses' kept soft (most suttas open evam me sutam; some do not). Confirm.
Chanting at funerals and house blessings (paritta): standard practice; confirm the howItsDone list.
Shape: senses (sound carries the idea; the practice is listening). Mai's storyline: ông wants her to chant with him in Pali before she leaves home.
Surprising fact: the suttas open with a listener's words, not the Buddha's: thus have I heard.
